intro:
**The Cosmic Swearing and the Purification of the Soul**

Ash-Shams, "The Sun," is the ninety-first chapter of the Qur'an, comprising 15 verses of early Makkan revelation. It holds an unique, peerless structural record in the sacred scripture: it opens with a majestic, contiguous cascade of *eleven consecutive cosmic and anthropological oaths*—the longest unbroken chain of oaths found anywhere in the Qur'an! (91:1–8 — *“By the sun and its brightness and the moon as it follows it and the day as it unveils it and the night as it conceals it And by heaven and ˹the One˺ Who built it and the earth and ˹the One˺ Who spread it And by the soul and ˹the One˺ Who fashioned it then with ˹the knowledge of˺ right and wrong inspired it”*). Swearing by the blazing sun, the reflecting moon, the unveiling day, the concealing night, the constructed heaven, the spread earth. The mysteriously proportioned human soul, the sūrah brings all of cosmic reality to bear upon a single, monumental ethical axiom in verses 9–10: *“He has certainly succeeded who purifies it [the soul], and he has certainly failed who buries / corrupts it!”* Characterized by exquisite, sonorous rhyming ending in the musical vowel *-hā*, Sūrah ash-Shams is the great scriptural manual on *Tazkiyah*—the conscious cultivation and purification of the human soul.

**The Structural Symmetry and the Hamstrung Camel**

The architecture of Sūrah ash-Shams is structured across two contrasting movements:

1. The Eleven Oaths and the Law of Tazkiyah (1–10): The eleven cosmic oaths culminating in the absolute definition of human success and failure: - *“He has certainly succeeded who purifies it (*qad aflaḥa man zakkāhā*)!”* - *“And he has certainly failed who corrupts / buries it (*wa-qad khāba man dassāhā*)!”*

2. The Historical Archetype: Thamūd and the She-Camel (11–15): Illustrates the catastrophe of *Dassāhā* (the corruption and burying of the soul) through the historic tragedy of Thamūd: their insolent rebellion drove them to challenge their prophet Ṣāliḥ, when the most wretched of them (*ashqāhā*) stepped forward to commit an unspeakable crime. The Messenger of Allah warned them: *“It is the she-camel of Allah and her turn to drink!”* But they rejected him and brutally hamstrung her (*fa-ʿaqarūhā*), whereupon their Lord crushed them for their crime and leveled them to the ground (*fa-damdama ʿalayhim Rabbuhum bi-dhanbihim fa-sawwāhā*). The chapter concludes with the chilling, sovereign declaration: *“And He does not fear the consequence of it (*wa-lā yakhāfu ʿuqbāhā*)!”*

verses.1:
> By the sun and its brightness

**Its Brightness, Not Only Its Body**

The oath names two things: the sun and its *ḍuḥā*. The second term is the light of the forenoon, the sun's brightness at its most diffused and useful. Swearing on the object and its quality is a deliberate doubling. The body of the sun is a fact of the sky; its brightness is what reaches the earth, what makes work possible and what the eye cannot hold. The doubling therefore moves the oath from the distant to the effective. A hearer may not think about the sun as a body, but he lives inside its brightness every hour of his working day. The verse captures both, and the second term is the one that touches him. The same word gave its name to the chapter of the Morning Light, where it was sworn on as the guarantee of a promise to a man accused of abandonment.

**The Sun in the Qur'an's Account of the World**

The Qur'an describes the sun with a consistency that suggests observation rather than poetry. "The sun and the moon ˹travel˺ with precision" (55:5). "The sun travels for its fixed term. That is the design of the Almighty, All-Knowing" (36:38). Its function in timekeeping is stated explicitly: God "made the sun a radiant source and the moon a reflected light, with precisely ordained phases, so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺" (10:5). The verse in this chapter swears on a body that the rest of the revelation describes as ordered, measured and purposive. The oath therefore carries an implicit claim: the greatest visible thing is not a god but a mechanism with a term, and swearing by it is a way of pointing past it to the One who set its term. The sun is described elsewhere in a fixed course, a measured journey and a light that serves a purpose, and this oath belongs to the same method. It does not treat the object as divine and it does not treat it as insignificant. It treats it as evidence.

**Swearing by Created Things, Not Worshipping Them**

The distinction between honouring a creature in an oath and worshipping it is one the Qur'an draws sharply. The same revelation that swears by the sun forbids prostration to it: "Among His signs are the day and the night, the sun and the moon. Do not prostrate to the sun or the moon, but prostrate to Allah, Who created them ˹all˺, if you ˹truly˺ worship Him ˹alone˺" (41:37). The verse places the sun inside the category of signs, which is the highest status a created thing holds in the Qur'an and the furthest from divinity. An oath on a sign magnifies the sign and, through it, the One who made it. The audience of this chapter included people who did worship the sun, and the oath is a correction addressed to them in the form of a solemnity.
verses.2:
> and the moon as it follows it

**Following Without Overtaking**

The verb in this verse describes a relation rather than a motion. *Talāhā* — it follows it — places the moon behind the sun in a sequence that never closes. The Qur'an states the rule elsewhere with precision: "It is not for the sun to catch up with the moon, nor does the night outrun the day. Each is travelling in an orbit of their own" (36:40). The following is therefore not a pursuit that might succeed. It is a permanent arrangement, and the permanence is what makes it worth swearing by. A relationship that could not be otherwise carries no moral information; a relationship that is maintained without ever being completed is a different thing, and it is the kind of order the chapter is invoking.

**The Crescent and the Reckoning of Time**

A second reading connects the verse to the new crescent, which appears at the start of each lunar month low in the west just after sunset and sets soon after the sun. The observation is exact, and it was part of the ordinary knowledge of the first audience, whose calendar depended on it. The Qur'an assigns the same function in the verse on timekeeping: the phases exist "so that you may know the number of years and calculation ˹of time˺" (10:5). The moon's following of the sun is so not only an astronomical fact but a practical one. It is how a community knows when to fast, when to make pilgrimage and when a debt falls due. An oath sworn on that relation invokes something the hearer uses every month of his life.

**Following as an Image of Submission**

The moon's obedience to its position is one instance of a claim the Qur'an makes about the whole created order: "To Allah ˹alone˺ bow down ˹in submission˺ all those in the heavens and the earth—willingly or unwillingly—as do their shadows, morning and evening" (13:15). The shadows are included, and the inclusion is instructive — even the incidental effects of bodies are described as submitting. The verse about the sun and the moon states their precision as a fact of design: "The sun and the moon ˹travel˺ with precision" (55:5). Neither body has ever deviated, and neither has been asked to. The following described in this verse is therefore a form of worship performed without intention, and it stands as a contrast to the creature that appears at the end of the chapter's oath list. A soul can refuse. The moon cannot. The comparison is not stated in the text, but the oath list arranges it, and the arrangement is what gives the final oath its force.

Surely in this are signs for those who understand" (16:12).
verses.3:
> and the day as it unveils it

**Jallāhā: An Act of Disclosure**

The verb in this verse is *jallā*, from a root meaning to unveil, to polish, to bring something into full view. It is stronger than "to show". A thing that is *jallā* has had its covering removed and is displayed in its clarity. Applied to the day, the verb describes what morning does: it takes a world that was hidden and makes it plain. The day is therefore not merely a period of time in this verse but an agent that performs an action. The grammar makes the day the subject of a verb of disclosure, and the object is what was earlier concealed. The oath is sworn on that act, which means the chapter is invoking revelation as a feature of the created order before it speaks of revelation as a book.

**The Day in the Qur'an's Pairing With the Night**

The day never appears alone in the Qur'an's oaths. The chapter that follows this one opens with the night when it covers and the day when it shines (92:1–2 — *“and the day when it shines”*), and the alternation is described elsewhere in the language of wrapping: "He wraps the night around the day, and wraps the day around the night" (39:5). The pairing is a sign in its own right, and the Qur'an says so: "Among His signs are the day and the night, the sun and the moon" (41:37). The verse in this chapter is one half of that pair, and its verb of disclosure gains its meaning from the verse that follows, whose verb is concealment. Neither verb can be understood alone, which is why the two oaths are joined. The pairing is consistent across the revelation and it is not accidental. The two are described as signs, as servants of a purpose and as successors of one another, and the reader who gathers those descriptions sees a single account rather than scattered remarks. The oath here is one item in that account.

**Disclosure as a Divine Act**

The day does not disclose itself. The Qur'an attributes the breaking of the dawn directly to God: "He causes the dawn to break, and has made the night for rest and ˹made˺ the sun and the moon ˹to travel˺ with precision. That is the design of the Almighty, All-Knowing" (6:96). The verse in this chapter swears by the day performing the act, and the following verses name the One who performs it through the day. The arrangement is characteristic: the created agent is honoured in the oath, and the Creator enters the oath immediately afterwards. A reader who stops at the day has missed the direction of the swearing, which is why the list continues for four more items before it reaches its object. Attributing the uncovering to God keeps the reader from treating it as an achievement. Light appears because it is made to appear, and the same holds for what the light stands for.
verses.4:
> and the night as it conceals it

**Ghashāhā: The Covering**

The verb that closes the first group of oaths is *ghashshā*, to cover, to veil, to draw something over a thing until it is hidden. It is the exact opposite of the verb in the previous verse, and the pairing is deliberate. The day unveils; the night covers. The same object is acted on in both cases, and the two acts are performed in turn without failure. The strength of the verb matters. A covering of this kind is complete: what is veiled is not dimmed but removed from sight. The night's action on the world is total, and the oath is sworn on that totality. The chapter is invoking the most complete concealment available in the visible order, and it will later use the image of covering for something a person does to himself.

**Concealment as a Provision, Not a Threat**

The night's covering is described elsewhere in the Qur'an as a mercy rather than as a menace. God "has made the night for rest" (6:96), and the alternation is presented as a design for the benefit of the creatures living inside it.

**The Night as the Hour of What Is Hidden**

Concealment has a moral dimension that the chapter exploits. The night is when acts are performed without witnesses, and the Qur'an's ethics distinguish sharply between the public and the private deed. It states the ranking plainly: "To give charity publicly is good, but to give to the poor privately is better for you, and will absolve you of your sins" (2:271). The hidden act is ranked above the visible one, and the ranking depends on the existence of a night in which hiding is possible. The verse's oath on concealment therefore touches the same ground. A world that covers its inhabitants makes sincerity possible, because it makes display optional. The chapter will argue that a soul can be buried under acts, and the image is drawn from this verb. Concealment has a hour, and the verse names it. What is hidden, deferred or done without witnesses belongs to this period, and the reader who recognises the pattern in his own week recognises why the night is worth swearing by. It is not a gap in the day but a distinct condition.
verses.5:
> And by heaven and ˹the One˺ Who built it

**The Grammatical Question: Who or What**

The Arabic word in these three verses is *mā*, which can function either as a relative meaning "the One who" or as a noun meaning "that which". Both readings are attested in the tradition. On the first, the verse reads as it is translated here: by the heaven and the One who built it. On the second, it reads "by the heaven and its building", making the oath completely about created things and avoiding the question of whether God can swear by Himself. Some exegetes preferred the second for exactly that reason, reasoning that a creature swearing by its Creator is fitting while a Creator swearing by Himself requires explanation. The first reading is the more natural in Arabic and is supported by the parallel constructions elsewhere in the Qur'an. The religious difficulty is not serious: God swears by what He wills, and swearing by His own action is a way of magnifying it.

**Banāhā: Building With Strength**

The verb is *banā*, to build, and the Qur'an uses the same verb of the heaven with an explicit statement of the manner: "We built the universe with ˹great˺ might, and We are certainly expanding ˹it˺" (51:47). The sūrah of the Draggers puts the act as a question that answers itself: "Which is harder to create: you or the sky? He built it, raising it high and forming it flawlessly" (79:27–28). The comparison in that verse is the point — the sky is offered as the greater of two creations, and the reader is expected to concede it. The oath in this chapter invokes that conceded greatness. A hearer who agrees that the sky is harder to make than he is has already granted the premise the chapter needs, and the premise is that the Maker of the sky is competent in matters he cannot see.

**A Roof Raised Without Supports**

The Qur'an's description of the heaven emphasises a feature that the naked eye confirms: it stands without visible support. "It is Allah Who has raised the heavens without pillars—as you can see— then established Himself on the Throne" (13:2). The clause "as you can see" is important, since it makes the claim an appeal to observation rather than to speculation. The verse in this chapter swears on a structure whose most striking feature is the absence of anything holding it up. The oath therefore invokes not only the size of the heaven but the nature of its maintenance. Something is being held in place by an arrangement the observer cannot see, and the chapter will shortly describe another such arrangement operating inside a human being.

The Qur'an joins the raising of the sky to the establishment of a balance: "As for the sky, He raised it ˹high˺, and set the balance ˹of justice˺" (55:7). The connection is not arbitrary.
verses.6:
> and the earth and ˹the One˺ Who spread it

**Ṭaḥāhā: Spreading a Habitable Surface**

The verb chosen for the earth is *ṭaḥā*, which describes the spreading out of a surface so that it can be used. The image is of a bed laid out or a hide stretched flat, and the Qur'an uses comparable language elsewhere: "As for the earth, He spread it out as well" (79:30). The sense is not that the earth is flat in a geometrical claim but that it has been made available — level enough to walk, stable enough to build on, extensive enough to sustain a population. The verse swears on that availability. A hearer standing on the ground is standing inside the object of the oath, and the swearing asks him to notice what he has never had to think about.

**The Same Grammatical Question as the Verse Before**

The word *mā* appears here again, and the two readings carry over: "the One who spread it" or "its spreading". The consistency across the three verses is evidence that a single construction is intended, and the parallelism of heaven and earth in the Qur'an supports the personal reading. The same pairing appears in the sūrah of the Winnowing Winds: "We built the universe with ˹great˺ might, and We are certainly expanding ˹it˺" (51:47), where the making of both realms is attributed to God in the first person. A reader who adopts the impersonal reading in one verse must adopt it in all three, which weakens the escalation the chapter is building. The personal reading preserves the movement from creation to Creator and is the stronger. The same grammatical question arises here as in the preceding verse, and the answer is the same. The maker is the one being sworn by, and the made thing is the occasion of the oath. The reader who settles the question once settles it for the whole series.

**Spreading as Provision**

The Qur'an does not describe the earth's preparation in neutral terms. It is described as provisioning. "He laid out the earth for all beings" (55:10), and the sūrah of the Draggers completes the sequence: spreading the earth, "bringing forth its water and pastures, and setting the mountains firmly ˹upon it˺— all as ˹a means of˺ sustenance for you and your animals" (79:30–33). The sūrah of al-Ḥijr says the same: "As for the earth, We spread it out and placed upon it firm mountains, and caused everything to grow there in perfect balance. And We made in it means of sustenance for you and others, who you do not provide for" (15:19–20). The last clause is the sharpest: some of the provision in the earth is for creatures the reader does not feed and does not know. The oath in this verse invokes a provision system wider than its beneficiary.

**A Sign Under the Reader's Feet**

The Qur'an repeatedly directs attention downward. "and the earth—how it was levelled out?" (88:20). "Have We not smoothed out the earth ˹like a bed˺, and ˹made˺ the mountains as ˹its˺ pegs" (78:6–7). The questions are rhetorical and they assume the answer is visible. The verse in this chapter belongs to that method, and its position in the oath list gives it weight. The heaven was named first because it is the greater; the earth is named second because it is the nearer. Between them the whole of the reader's physical world has been sworn by, and both have been attached to a Maker. The argument is now complete at the level of the visible, and the next verse leaves the visible completely. The sign is under the reader's feet, which is what makes it unavoidable. He cannot decline to notice it by looking away, and he cannot postpone it by claiming ignorance. The verse is built on the impossibility of evading this particular piece of evidence.

It is the place of provision: "And We made in it means of sustenance for you and others, who you do not provide for" (15:20).
verses.7:
> And by the soul and ˹the One˺ Who fashioned it

**The Last Object of the Oath Cannot Be Seen**

Six objects have been sworn by, and every one of them is visible: light, a following body, a disclosing day, a covering night, a built heaven, a spread earth. The seventh is none of these. The soul has no horizon, no orbit and no season, and the reader cannot step outside to look at it. The placement is the argument. The chapter has spent six oaths establishing that the visible order is made, ordered and purposive, and it now applies the same claim to the one thing the reader knows better than anything in the sky and cannot observe at all.

**Sawwāhā: Fashioned in Proportion**

The verb is *sawwā*, which means to make level, to proportion, to bring a thing into its proper shape. The Qur'an uses the same verb of the human being directly: God is the One "Who created you, fashioned you, and perfected your design" (82:7). The sūrah of the Fig states the result: "Indeed, We created humans in the best form" (95:4). The claim is that the soul is not a residue or an accident but a construction, and a construction implies a constructor with an intention. The verse in this chapter names both in a single phrase — the soul and the One who fashioned it — and the pairing is the same one used for the heaven and the earth. What is true of the cosmos is true of the person: it was made, and it was made by design.

**The Three Souls the Qur'an Names**

The Qur'an describes the soul in three states, and the three together define the range in which this chapter's argument operates. The soul at peace is addressed at the end of the sūrah of the Dawn: "O tranquil soul! Return to your Lord, well pleased ˹with Him˺ and well pleasing ˹to Him˺" (89:27). The self-reproaching soul is sworn by in the sūrah of the Resurrection: "And I do swear by the self-reproaching soul!" (75:2). The third is described by Yūsuf's wife in a confession: "indeed the soul is ever inclined to evil, except those shown mercy by my Lord" (12:53). The three are not three souls but three conditions of one soul, and the movement between them is what the next two verses describe. A soul can be cultivated toward peace, left in self-reproach, or allowed to follow its inclination.

**Fiṭrah: An Orientation Given at Creation**

The fashioning described in this verse is not neutral. The Qur'an describes human beings as created with an orientation already in place: "the natural Way of Allah which He has instilled in ˹all˺ people. Let there be no change in this creation of Allah" (30:30). The soul is therefore fashioned toward something, and the fashioning is the ground on which the command to purify it can be issued. A soul with no orientation could not be purified, since purification implies a standard; a soul oriented toward evil alone could not be blamed for following it.

**A Verb the Chapter Will Use Again**

*Sawwā* appears once more in this chapter, and its second appearance is grim. The same verb used for fashioning the soul is used for what happened to the tribe that destroyed itself: their Lord crushed them and levelled them (91:14 — *“Still they defied him and slaughtered her. So their Lord crushed them for their crime, levelling all to the ground”*). The wordplay is not accidental. The One who proportioned a soul is the One who can flatten a civilisation, and the two acts are performed by the same hand with the same ease. The chapter places the two uses eleven verses apart and leaves the reader to make the connection. A soul fashioned with such care can be buried by its owner, and a people who bury theirs can be levelled by their Maker. The verb holds both statements together. The verb introduced here returns later in the chapter, and the return is where the argument closes. A reader who notes the introduction will recognise the reuse and will understand that the two occurrences describe one process from two ends. The chapter depends on that recognition.
verses.8:
> then with ˹the knowledge of˺ right and wrong inspired it

**Alhamahā: Instilled, Not Taught**

The verb in this verse is *alhama*, from a root meaning to cause something to be present in a mind without instruction. It is the verb of inspiration in the strict sense: knowledge that arrives without a teacher, without a text and without an argument. The object is twofold — its *fujūr* and its *taqwā*, its wrongdoing and its reverence — and both are given together. The verse therefore claims that every human being arrives equipped with a recognition of the difference between the two, before any revelation reaches him and before any argument is put to him. The claim is bold, and its boldness is what the chapter needs, since the argument that follows holds every person responsible. Instilling is not teaching, and the difference is what the verse turns on.

**Knowledge That Precedes Revelation**

The claim of this verse is that moral recognition is before scripture. The Qur'an states the same priority elsewhere, in the account of a covenant taken before birth: "And ˹remember˺ when your Lord brought forth from the loins of the children of Adam their descendants and had them testify about themselves. ˹Allah asked,˺ ‘Am I not your Lord?’ They replied, ‘Yes, You are!’" (7:172). The purpose of that testimony is stated in the same verse: so that nobody can plead ignorance on the Day of Judgment. The two verses belong together. A covenant taken in advance and a knowledge instilled at creation produce the same result — no person can claim that the distinction was never shown to him. The chapter's own list of endowments in the sūrah of the City makes the same point from the other direction, where humanity is described as shown "the two ways ˹of right and wrong˺" (90:10).

**The Report on Decree and This Verse**

The verse has been at the centre of a discussion about destiny since the earliest generations. A report preserved in both principal collections records a man asking the Prophet ﷺ whether the people of Paradise and the people of the Fire are already distinguished, and — on being told that they are — asking what use deeds then have. The answer was: "Everyone will be facilitated to that for which he was created" (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 6596; Ṣaḥīḥ Muslim 2649). The commentators connect that answer to this verse, since the facilitation described is the working out of the two capacities instilled here. The connection does not resolve the tension between decree and choice, and the report does not claim to. What it establishes is that the two terms are not treated as alternatives in the Prophet's own teaching. A person is facilitated toward what he was made for, and he is still commanded to act.
verses.9:
> Successful indeed is the one who purifies their soul

**The Answer the Oaths Were Taken For**

Seven oaths, and then a single sentence. The verse delivers what the swearing guaranteed, and the delivery is short enough to memorise: successful indeed is the one who purifies it. The emphatic particle at the head of the sentence marks the statement as settled, and the indefinite subject — whoever, the one who — makes it apply to anyone. Nothing in the verse restricts the promise to a community, a time or a class. The seven objects sworn by, descending from the sun to the soul, exist to give this sentence its weight, and the sentence turns out to be about conduct rather than about the order of the universe. The answer is short because the oaths were long.

**Purification as the Revelation's Own Programme**

The Qur'an describes its own purpose in these terms. The mission of the messenger is summarised as "reciting to them His revelations, purifying them. Teaching them the Book and wisdom" (3:164), and the same threefold description appears in the prayer of Abraham for the city's future (2:129 — *“Our Lord! Raise from among them a messenger who will recite to them Your revelations, teach them the Book and wisdom, and purify them.”*) and in the account of what was done for a people who had earlier been astray (62:2 — *“He is the One Who raised for the illiterate ˹people˺ a messenger from among themselves—reciting to them His revelations, purifying them, and teaching them the Book and wisdom, for indeed they had previously been clearly astray”*). The reminder to the believers repeats it: "Since We have sent you a messenger from among yourselves—reciting to you Our revelations, purifying you, teaching you the Book and wisdom" (2:151). The verb in this verse is the same verb that appears in all of those passages. The chapter's central statement is therefore not an isolated aphorism but a compressed statement of the revelation's purpose. The programme is stated elsewhere in the same terms, and the consistency is what makes it a programme rather than an aspiration. A reader who meets the same verb applied to property, to conduct and to the soul understands that one process is being described in three settings.

**Who Purifies: The Ambiguity of the Subject**

Some of the earliest commentators read the verse with God as the subject: he whose soul God purifies has succeeded. The reading is supported by verses that attribute purification to God alone, and it guards against a theology of self-enough effort. The opposite error is equally guarded against elsewhere: "Indeed, Allah would never change a people's state ˹of favour˺ until they change their own state ˹of faith˺" (13:11). The two statements stand together, and the ambiguity of the subject in this verse holds them in place. A reader who attributes the purification completely to himself has misread the oaths that precede it, since the soul's Maker is named in the seventh. A reader who waits for the purification without acting has misread the verb, which is in the active voice and describes work.
verses.10:
> and doomed is the one who corrupts it

**Dassāhā: To Bury**

The verb in this verse is *dassā*, and its root means hiding, burying, pressing something into the ground until it disappears. The Qur'an uses the same verb for the most extreme act of concealment in its pages: the man given the news of a daughter's birth who deliberates "should he keep her in disgrace, or bury her ˹alive˺ in the ground?" (16:59). The verb therefore carries an image, and the image is violent. Applied to the soul, it describes not a failure to improve but an act of interment. The soul is not only neglected in this verse; it is put under. The choice of verb is the sharpest feature of the statement, and it rules out any reading in which the failure is passive. Burying implies concealment from sight and effort spent on the concealment, and both features belong to the verse. A person does not bury something carelessly; he covers it so that it will not be found. The reader who recognises the effort will recognise the pattern in his own conduct.

**The Soul Will Testify**

The concealment described in this verse does not succeed in its aim. The Qur'an states the outcome plainly: "In fact, people will testify against their own souls, despite the excuses they come up with" (75:14–15). The buried soul is not lost; it is present as a witness against the one who buried it. The verse therefore adds a second layer to the warning. A person can cover what he was made with, and the covering will not hold at the moment it matters. The excuses mentioned in that verse are the ordinary ones — circumstance, other people, ignorance — and the verse dismisses them in advance. The reader who is burying his soul is accumulating testimony against himself, and the testimony is his own. The soul testifies rather than being judged by a stranger, and the arrangement is what makes the outcome undeniable. A reader who disputes an external accusation can continue disputing it; he cannot dispute his own knowledge of what he did. The verse places the evidence where it cannot be challenged.
verses.11:
> Thamûd rejected ˹the truth˺ out of arrogance

**Ṭaghwāhā: The Rejection Had a Manner**

The verse does not simply say that Thamūd rejected. It says they rejected *bi-ṭaghwāhā* — in their transgression, through their overstepping. The addition specifies the character of the refusal. This was not a failure of evidence or a hesitation of intellect. It was an act of a people who knew what was being asked and refused on grounds of their own standing. The Qur'an's account of the same rejection elsewhere supports the reading: "As for Thamûd, We showed them guidance, but they preferred blindness over guidance" (41:17). The verb of preference is decisive. Guidance was shown and blindness was chosen, and the choosing is described as an act of will rather than a state of ignorance. The word in this verse names the will behind it. The manner of the rejection matters because rejection is not a single act. It was excessive, and the excess is what the verse names rather than the fact alone. The reader who has been treating his own refusals as isolated incidents is being shown that refusal has a shape and a direction.

**Who They Were and Where They Lived**

Thamūd were a northern Arabian tribe, and their settlement is named in the Qur'an as the Stone Valley: "Indeed, the residents of the Stone Valley also denied the messengers" (15:80). Their distinguishing achievement is recorded in the challenge put to them by their messenger: "to carve homes in the mountains with great skill?" (26:149). The site lies on the caravan route between the Ḥijāz and Syria, and it was still occupied by ruins in the Prophet's lifetime. Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī records that when the army passed through the land of Thamūd called al-Ḥijr, the Prophet ﷺ ordered his companions to pour out the water they had drawn from its wells and to take water only from the well the she-camel used to drink from (Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī 3378). The place was not a legend to the first audience. It was a location they passed.

**The Rejection Recorded Across the Revelation**

The story appears repeatedly, and the repetitions are evidence of its familiarity. The sūrah of the Moon opens its account with the same verb: "Thamûd rejected the warnings ˹as well˺" (54:23). The sūrah of the Ant describes the internal division the messenger produced: "We certainly sent to the people of Thamûd their brother Ṣâliḥ, proclaiming, ‘Worship Allah,’ but they suddenly split into two opposing groups" (27:45). The longer Meccan and Madinan accounts in Sūrahs 7 and 11 expand the narrative with speeches on both sides. The chapter in front of us compresses all of it into five verses, which it can do only because the audience already knows the story. The compression is a sign of confidence in the hearer's memory. The record is spread across the revelation, and the spread is what makes the account reliable. A reader who finds the same event described in several chapters with consistent details understands that he is not reading a passing allusion but a documented case referred to deliberately.
verses.12:
> when the most wicked of them was roused ˹to kill the she-camel˺

**Inbaʿatha: Sent Forth by Others**

The verb is *inbaʿatha*, to be roused, dispatched, to rise to a task at the prompting of others. The man did not act alone and he did not act first. The Qur'an states the arrangement explicitly in the sūrah of the Moon: "But they roused a companion of theirs, so he dared to kill ˹her˺" (54:29). The verse in this chapter uses a passive construction that preserves the same fact: he was roused. Somebody sent him. The passive voice is doing moral work, since it records that the tribe produced the act even though one hand performed it. The reader is shown the mechanism by which a community commits a crime through an agent, and the mechanism is why the whole community is punished.

**The Nine Men of the City**

The Qur'an supplies the social context elsewhere. "And there were in the city nine ˹elite˺ men who spread corruption in the land, never doing what is right" (27:48). The description is precise: a small group of notables, corrupt, and opposed to reform. The man who hamstrung the camel came from that milieu, and the verse in this chapter identifies him as the worst among them. The detail matters for the application. Societies are not destroyed by the wickedness of their weakest members but by the wickedness of those with standing, because standing is what allows a private vice to become a public act. The chapter names the ringleader and leaves the reader to look for the equivalent in his own city.

**The Name and the Report**

The interpretive tradition names the man Qudār ibn Sālif, and the name appears in the earliest commentaries. A report preserved in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī, in the Book of Commentary, describes the one who went forth to the camel as a strong, mighty man, invincible among his people, and compares him to Abū Zamʿah. The description is not incidental. The man chosen for the task was chosen for his capacity to perform it without being stopped, which means the tribe's selection was practical as well as moral. They sent someone who could not be resisted. The verse's superlative — the most wretched — is therefore matched by a superlative of force, and the combination is what made the crime possible. The name is preserved in the interpretive record, and the preservation is worth noting because the Qur'an itself does not give it. A reader who knows the name from the tradition knows that the identification is transmitted rather than revealed, and the distinction affects how much weight the detail carries.

**A Collective Crime With a Single Hand**

The punishment that follows falls on the whole tribe, and the arrangement has puzzled readers. A man who is roused acts as the hand of those who roused him, and the tribe's approval is recorded in the account: they called their companion and he took up the task.
verses.13:
> But the messenger of Allah warned them, “˹Do not disturb˺ Allah’s camel and her ˹turn to˺ drink!”

**The Warning Given in Full Elsewhere**

This chapter compresses the messenger's warning into a single sentence, and the longer accounts supply the rest. Ṣâliḥ's words are recorded at length in the sūrah of Hūd: "And O my people! This she-camel of Allah is a sign for you. So leave her to graze ˹freely˺ on Allah's earth and do her no harm, or a swift punishment will overtake you!" (11:64). The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf adds the ground of the claim: "A clear proof has come to you from your Lord: this is Allah's she-camel as a sign to you" (7:73). The compressed form in this chapter preserves the two essential elements — the animal belongs to God, and her drinking is to be respected — and omits the rest because the audience already had it. The compression is a sign that the story was common knowledge.

**The Division of the Water**

The specific term of the test was an arrangement about water. Ṣâliḥ states it in the sūrah of the Poets: "Here is a camel. She will have her turn to drink as you have yours, each on an appointed day" (26:155). The sūrah of the Moon records the same instruction: "And tell them that the ˹drinking˺ water must be divided between them ˹and her˺, each taking a turn to drink ˹every other day˺" (54:28). The arrangement is precise and modest. Nobody was asked to surrender his water completely; everybody was asked to alternate. The test was therefore not a demand for sacrifice but a demand for fairness, and the fairness had a schedule. A people who could not keep a rota for a well had failed something much smaller than a religious system. Dividing the water is the clearest possible form of the arrangement, and the verse chooses it because water cannot be shared ambiguously. A reader who has seen a community allocate a scarce resource understands the arrangement immediately, and the understanding is what makes the demand that follows so stark.

**A Sign, Not an Object of Worship**

The camel was not presented as something to be venerated. It was presented as a sign — evidence that the messenger spoke for God. The Qur'an is explicit: "this is Allah's she-camel as a sign to you" (7:73), and in the sūrah of the Moon the sending is described as a test: "We are sending the she-camel as a test for them. So watch them ˹closely˺, and have patience" (54:27). The animal's function was evidential, and the command attached to it was negative: do not harm her. Nothing in the arrangement required belief in the camel, ritual directed at her, or expenditure on her behalf. The whole of the demand was restraint. That is why the crime is so damaging in the chapter's argument. A people who cannot refrain from harming an animal they have been told to leave alone have failed the smallest possible test.
verses.14:
> Still they defied him and slaughtered her. So their Lord crushed them for their crime, levelling all to the ground

**Fa-ʿaqqarūhā: The Method of the Killing**

The verb describes hamstringing — cutting the tendons of the leg so that the animal collapses and cannot rise. It is not the ordinary word for slaughter, and the choice is significant. Hamstringing is done to a creature that one intends to leave helpless, and it is the method used when the killer wants the animal down before it is finished. The Qur'an uses the same verb elsewhere in the account: "Then they killed the she-camel —defying their Lord's command—" (7:77). The specificity of the word preserves the brutality of the act, and the brutality is part of the chapter's argument. This was not an utilitarian killing for meat. It was a public destruction of a sign, performed in a way that maximised the animal's helplessness before witnesses. The method of the killing is specified, and the specification is not incidental. Hamstringing an animal destroys it without benefit to anyone, and the reader who knows what the method involves understands that the act was destruction rather than necessity. The verse records the manner because the manner is the crime.

**Damdama ʿAlayhim: A Punishment That Covered Them**

The verb used for the punishment is *damdama*, and the commentators describe it as the most severe form of destruction: something that comes suddenly, annihilates and covers completely. The reduplication in the root conveys intensity and repetition, and the preposition "upon them" completes the image — the punishment came down over them rather than at them. The Qur'an describes the same event in other terms elsewhere. The sūrah of Hūd records the blast: "And the ˹mighty˺ blast overtook the wrongdoers, so they fell lifeless in their homes, as if they had never lived there" (11:67–68). The sūrah of al-Aʿrāf records an earthquake: "Then an ˹overwhelming˺ earthquake struck them, and they fell lifeless in their homes" (7:78). The verse in this chapter compresses all of it into a single verb of crushing.

**The Three Days Between the Act and the End**

The fuller account supplies a detail this verse omits, and the detail matters. After the killing, Ṣâliḥ told them: "You have ˹only˺ three ˹more˺ days to enjoy life in your homes— this is an unfailing promise!" (11:65). The interval was announced, and it elapsed. The punishment was therefore not a surprise sprung on a people who might have repented; it was a dated event, communicated in advance, which they spent in their homes. The three days are the chapter's most severe detail, because they remove the last excuse. A people given a deadline and a warning, who use the time neither to repent nor to flee, have made their position final. The crushing described in this verse arrived at the end of a period they had been told about. Three days is a period the reader can hold in mind, and the period is what makes the account concrete.
verses.15:
> He has no fear of consequences

**The Warning to the Audience in Mecca**

The application to the first hearers is direct. A people who had been given a messenger, a sign and a warning had been destroyed, and the One who destroyed them feared nothing. The Quraysh were in the same position: a messenger among them, a book as the sign, and an opposition that had begun to resemble the transgression of Thamūd. The verse tells them what stands behind the warning. It is not a threat issued by a man who can be resisted or a faction that can be outlasted. It is a statement about a power that has already exercised itself on a people stronger in their buildings than the Quraysh, and that was unaffected by the exercise. The chapter's final sentence is therefore a warning delivered in the grammatical form of a description.

**The Third Reading: The Messenger's Completed Duty**

On the third reading the subject is Ṣâliḥ, and the verse records that he did not fear the outcome because he had done what he was sent to do. The Qur'an describes the same posture after the punishment in the sūrah of al-Aʿrāf: "So he turned away from them, saying, ‘O my people! Surely I conveyed to you my Lord's message and gave you ˹sincere˺ advice, but you do not like ˹sincere˺ advisors’" (7:79). The messenger's freedom from fear is the freedom of a person who has discharged an obligation completely. The reading has the advantage of ending the chapter on the messenger rather than on the punishment, and it fits the pattern of the Qur'an's accounts, in which the prophet is spared and speaks after the destruction. It is the least common of the three readings and the most consoling.
